registered.old: Read actual assumption of risk, contractual clauses, and the allocation implied by the deal and law. Stees construed the building promise strictly despite quicksand. For force majeure, apply trigger, causation, notice, mitigation and relief specified by the language.
registered.new: Read actual assumption of risk, contractual clauses, and the allocation implied by the deal and law. For mistake, a party bears the risk when the agreement allocates it, when he knew at formation that his knowledge was limited and treated it as sufficient (conscious ignorance), or when the court allocates it as reasonable (§ 154); courts generally allocate to a seller of farm land the risk that it holds valuable minerals (C&M 1081 Note 2) and to a builder the cost of draining subsoil (§ 154 illus. 5). Stees construed the building promise strictly despite quicksand; where the owner supplied a design specification prescribing design, materials and methods, courts treat it as impliedly warranting their adequacy (Spearin, C&M 1077 Note 2). For force majeure, apply trigger, causation, notice, mitigation and relief specified by the language: general words after a list may be confined to similar events (ejusdem generis), a clause covering an event may not cover its economic aftermath, and an express exclusion such as a duty to pay rent regardless controls (C&M 1117–1119).
registered.reason: § 154 allocates the risk by agreement, by conscious ignorance ('aware ... that he has only limited knowledge ... but treats his limited knowledge as sufficient'), or by the court; Stees Note 2 says a design specification 'impliedly warrants their adequacy' (C&M 1077); the force-majeure notes turn on ejusdem generis, economic aftermath and a rent proviso (C&M 1117–1119). Node d named none of these.

registered.old: Mistake can justify avoidance and restoration. A later event may discharge or suspend remaining duties, depending on doctrine or clause. Renner restored payment and net value conferred, rather than every development expense.
registered.new: Mistake can justify avoidance and restoration (§§ 158, 376). A later event may discharge or suspend remaining duties, depending on doctrine or clause; a temporary impediment suspends the duty and discharges it only if later performance would be materially more burdensome (§ 269). After discharge, either party may claim restitution for benefits conferred by part performance or reliance (§§ 272(1), 377), and a court may protect reliance where those rules will not avoid injustice (§§ 158(2), 272(2)). Renner, applying Arizona law, restored payment and net value conferred, rather than every development expense. Taylor's promoters could not recover preparation expenses as damages for breach (C&M 1105), and Transatlantic said that a carrier whose contract was a nullity would claim quantum meruit for the entire voyage, not only the extra cost on top of the collected price (C&M 1112).
registered.reason: § 272(1) and § 377 give restitution for benefits conferred by part performance or reliance after discharge, and §§ 158(2), 272(2) let a court protect reliance only where those rules 'will not avoid injustice'; Transatlantic: the claim 'should have been quantum meruit for the entire trip, rather than only for the extra expense' (C&M 1112). Node g gave no rule for relief after discharge.

mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullNew:
Renner involved land and water conditions essential to the parties’ intended agricultural use. The court treated the mistaken basic assumption as grounds for rescission and then addressed restitution separately. Stees illustrates a different treatment of an undertaking to achieve a construction result despite unexpected difficulty.

Ask what fact was mistaken, whether the mistake was shared, whether it materially affected the exchange, and whether the contract or governing rule allocated the risk. A mistaken prediction about later profitability is not automatically the same as a mistake about an existing basic fact. The remedy also requires care: unwinding the exchange and compensating every expenditure are not identical. If only one party was mistaken, that party may avoid only by meeting every § 152 requirement, not bearing the risk under § 154, and showing that enforcement would be unconscionable or that the other party had reason to know of the mistake or his fault caused it (§ 153 and cmt. b). Erroneous construction bids are the usual case (Elsinore v. Kastorff, C&M 1081); a bidder's misjudgment of the labor required is a risk the court allocates to the bidder (§ 154 illus. 6). The parol evidence rule does not bar prior agreements or negotiations offered to show that the parties were mistaken (§ 152 cmt. a; Stees Note 4, C&M 1078).

mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullNew:
Taylor concerns destruction of the specific music hall essential to the performances. Transatlantic concerns closure of the Suez Canal when the ship could still complete the voyage by a longer route. That contrast makes the promised performance and available alternatives central. Increased cost or difficulty does not automatically establish an excuse.

Identify the event, its effect on the actual undertaking, the assumption on which the parties contracted, the allocation of risk, and any fault or contractual clause affecting the analysis. The casebook also discusses more recent disruptions as applications to test; their treatment depends on the particular contract. Keep impossibility of the performance distinct from a decline in the value the recipient expects to obtain. In a sale of goods, UCC § 2-613 avoids the contract when goods identified at formation suffer a total casualty without fault before risk of loss passes; § 2-614(1) requires a commercially reasonable substitute manner of delivery to be tendered and accepted; and § 2-615 excuses a seller for a contingency whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption, if the seller allocates partial capacity fairly and notifies the buyer seasonably. Increased cost alone does not excuse (cmt. 4), and a failed source excuses only a seller who took all due measures to assure it would not fail (cmt. 5, citing Canadian Industrial Alcohol). An impracticability that is only temporary suspends the duty while it lasts and discharges it only if later performance would be materially more burdensome (§ 269); Gene Autry's interruption of his studio contract for wartime service was not a breach (C&M 1131–1132).

mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullNew:
In Krell, rooms could still be supplied, but cancellation of the coronation procession defeated the shared purpose for which the particular daytime use had been arranged. The court considered the transaction’s setting and the parties’ understanding rather than requiring an express sentence naming that purpose.

A party’s private hope or ordinary loss of profit does not necessarily define the bargain’s principal purpose. Determine whether the purpose was sufficiently shared or known, whether the disruption was fundamental, and whether the party claiming excuse bore the risk. Distinguish frustration from impossibility: the former asks what performance would now achieve, while the latter asks whether the undertaking can be performed. Frustration 'is not a form of impossibility': performance remains possible, but its expected value to the party seeking excuse has been destroyed (Lloyd v. Murphy, quoted at C&M 1135). Krell's Derby Day dictum marks the limit: a cab hired at an enhanced price for the race is not discharged if the race is cancelled, because any other cab would have done as well (C&M 1134). The problems at C&M 1136 test that line with lodging booked at more than double the usual rate for a homecoming cancelled after a tornado, and with a nearly finished wedding dress after the intended spouse's fatal accident; relief for part performance follows § 272.

mapEntryRunTimeEdits (tools/r19/data/r21.fullNew:
Allocation may be expressed through conditions, warranties, fixed prices, or force-majeure clauses. It may also follow from the undertaking interpreted in context and the governing legal rules. Stees, Taylor, Transatlantic, and Krell illustrate different relationships among the promised result, the disrupted circumstances, and the claimed excuse.

Foreseeability is relevant, but asking whether an event could have been imagined does not finish the inquiry. A party may know a risk exists without clearly assuming every consequence; conversely, an unconditional undertaking may place a risk on that party. Explain the language, commercial purpose, alternatives, and burden rather than using “risk” as an unexplained label. Foreseeability is 'at best but one fact to be considered' (Wolf Trap, C&M 1115). An event foreshadowed at contracting may be among the dickered risks (UCC § 2-615 cmt. 8): a settlement signed the day schools closed for COVID-19 was not excused by the pandemic's later financial effects (Belk, C&M 1115). A seller that promotes a 'revolutionary' system bears the risk that the breakthrough cannot be built (Wegematic, C&M 1113). The superior-risk-bearer analysis asks which party could better estimate, insure against or spread the loss, avert the event or mitigate it (C&M 1116–1117).

new.label: Does a fact existing at formation excuse under § 266?
new.detail: Where, when the contract is made, a party's performance is impracticable, or his principal purpose is substantially frustrated, without his fault because of a fact of which he has no reason to know and whose non-existence is a basic assumption, no duty to render that performance arises, unless the language or circumstances indicate the contrary (§ 266). The 'no reason to know' requirement is stricter than mistake, where a party's fault in failing to discover the facts bars avoidance only if it amounts to a failure to act in good faith and in accordance with reasonable standards of fair dealing (§ 157). The casebook's example is gravel on the land that could be removed only at prohibitive cost (Mineral Park, C&M 1100–1101), and a buyer whose dredge proves unfit for a purpose both parties assumed may have § 266(2) relief though the mistake is not material (§ 152 cmt. c, illus. 9).
